text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNLinearize continuity, momentum, and Poisson equations, derive the Jeans length and growth time, and explain the limits of subtracting background gravity. Connect to foundations: The virial theorem: why shrinking stars heat up ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Two responses compete in a compression A small overdensity attracts additional gas, while its pressure increase tends to erase the contrast. Examine individual wavelengths to determine where gravity wins. Exclude rotation, magnetic fields, viscosity, and expansion of the background in this model. ρ = ρ₀(1+δ), P = P₀+cs²ρ₀δ cs² = (∂P∂ρ)background The density contrast δ is dimensionless and satisfies |δ| ≪ 1. Isothermal and adiabatic responses have different sound speeds. Use the constant cs appropriate to the chosen closure rather than silently switching between them. 02What happened to background gravity? An infinite uniform density at rest creates a background problem: its pressure gradient vanishes, but ordinary Poisson gravity requires ∇²Φ₀ = 4πGρ₀, not zero. A static homogeneous background with zero gravitational field is not self-consistent without an additional prescription. Define a background-subtracted local model with ∇²φ = 4πG(ρ−ρ₀). The treatment of background gravity is the issue behind the Jeans swindle. Cosmological perturbations include Hubble damping and are not governed by the same static-background equation. To solve a finite cloud with its boundary conditions, use a different model such as a Bonnor–Ebert sphere. The purpose here is the local competition between pressure and gravity at each wavelength. 03Eliminate velocity from three equations Let u denote perturbation velocity. Linearize continuity and momentum, discarding quadratic terms such as δu. Differentiate continuity in time and substitute the divergence of momentum to obtain an equation for density contrast alone. ∂δ∂t+∇·u = 0 ∂u∂t = −cs²∇δ−∇φ, ∇²φ = 4πGρ₀δ ∂²δ∂t² = cs²∇²δ+4πGρ₀δ The gravitational term reinforces a density peak. The spatial second derivative of a wave is negative at that peak, so the sound-speed term restores it. Checking these derivative signs explains the competition without memorizing the final criterion. 04Replace derivatives with wavenumber and frequency Insert a plane wave δ = δ₁exp[i(k·r−ωt)]. The second time derivative supplies −ω² and the Laplacian supplies −k². Positive ω² gives oscillations; negative ω² allows growing and decaying solutions with ω = iσ. ω² = cs²k²−4πGρ₀ kJ = √(4πGρ₀)cs, λJ = 2πkJ = cs√(πGρ₀) Wavelengths longer than λJ are unstable. At short wavelengths the pressure term increases as k². The exact k = 0 mode changes the mean density and is excluded from the background-subtracted perturbations; the plotted long-wave endpoint is a formal limit. 05Define length, mass, and time separately MJ ≡ 4π3ρ₀(λJ2)³ = π5/26cs³G3/2ρ₀1/2 tJ ≡ 1√(4πGρ₀), σtJ = √[1−(k/kJ)²] The numerical coefficient in a Jeans mass depends on the geometry and length used to convert a wavelength into mass. Here the sphere’s radius is half a wavelength. The wavelength criterion itself follows directly from the dispersion relation. When δ approaches order unity, the omitted nonlinear terms matter. A linear growth rate does not predict the number or masses of the eventual stars. For a rotating thin disk, include the rotational response as in Toomre Q. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed sound speed, quadruple density. How do Jeans wavelength, the mass convention used here, and the gravitational timescale change? Show the answer and reasoning All three scale as ρ₀−1/2, so all halve. The mass here is that of a sphere of radius λJ/2. Defining it as ρλJ³ changes a numerical coefficient, not its density and sound-speed scaling. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text. Falco et al.
